title: 2. What the Company Does: Segments, Revenue Mix & Concrete Examples

epigraph.quote: Regeneron delivered another quarter of strong financial performance, with double-digit top- and bottom-line growth reflecting the continued strength of our commercial portfolio and the potential of our pipeline.
epigraph.author: Dr. Leonard Schleifer, Co-Founder, President & CEO

web_blocks.html: Regeneron reports as one combined drug segment, yet its sales flow through five clear engines [1, 2, 3]. First is U.S. Ophthalmology (Eylea & Eylea HD), where Regeneron books 100% of U.S. net sales. Second is the Sanofi Antibody Collaboration (Dupixent & Kevzara). Sanofi records global net sales, while Regeneron books its profit share and drug-supply payments. Third is Global Oncology (Libtayo), where Regeneron books 100% of global net sales and pays Sanofi a small royalty. Fourth is the Bayer Collaboration (Ex-U.S. Eylea), where Bayer sells aflibercept abroad and splits profits with Regeneron. Fifth is Other Commercial Products & Royalties, which covers U.S. Praluent, Evkeeza, Veopoz, Ordspono, Lynozyfic, and Ilaris/Arcalyst royalties [1, 2, 3].

web_blocks.takeaway: Regeneron's revenue center of gravity has shifted decisively from U.S. Eylea 2 mg to Dupixent (41% of FY25 revenue, surging higher post-Q2 2026), Eylea HD, and Libtayo.

web_blocks.html: Walkthrough 1 — U.S. Ophthalmology (Eylea & Eylea HD): Picture a 74-year-old retired teacher with blurred central vision from wet age-related macular degeneration. At a local retina clinic, an optical coherence tomography (OCT) scan spots fluid behind the retina. The doctor does not write a retail script. Instead, the clinic pulls a chilled vial of Eylea HD (aflibercept 8 mg) from its own fridge, bought upfront from McKesson or CuraScript SD under the "buy-and-bill" model [17, 18]. After numbing the eye, the doctor gives a 0.07 mL shot in a 10-minute office visit. The clinic then bills Medicare Part B under a permanent J-code at Average Sales Price (ASP) plus 6% (4.3% after sequestration), plus a visit fee [19]. Eylea HD keeps vision sharp with shots spaced up to every 16 to 20 weeks after loading doses [8]. Older 2 mg shots require visits every 4 to 8 weeks. As a result, patients cut annual eye-clinic trips in half, and Regeneron books 100% of the U.S. net wholesale price [8]. Outside the U.S., Bayer runs the same model across Europe and Asia. Bayer splits net profits 50/50 (with tiered rates in Japan) and paid Regeneron $139.7 million in FY2025 for commercial drug supply [2].

Walkthrough 2 — Sanofi Immunology Collaboration (Dupixent & Kevzara): Next, picture a 58-year-old former machinist with severe COPD driven by type 2 inflammation. He still suffers frequent flare-ups despite using three inhaled drugs [13]. His lung doctor prescribes Dupixent (dupilumab), which blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signals [13]. Unlike Eylea, Dupixent moves through a specialty pharmacy like CVS Specialty or Accredo under the pharmacy benefit. Once insurance clears blood-eosinophil and inhaler checks, the pharmacy ships a cold 300 mg prefilled pen to the patient's home every two weeks. Sanofi books the global sale ($17.81 billion in FY2025; $6.5 billion in Q3 2026, with U.S. sales topping $5.1 billion) [2, 3]. Regeneron makes the bulk drug in Rensselaer and Limerick and collects cost paybacks ($642.4 million in FY2025). It splits U.S. profits 50/50 with Sanofi and shares tiered ex-U.S. profits, alongside Kevzara's $574.6 million in global sales [12]. As of Q2 2026, the 20% development-balance deduction is gone [12].

Walkthrough 3 — Global Oncology & Specialty Portfolio (Libtayo, Bispecifics & Rare Diseases): Finally, consider a 68-year-old patient with advanced skin cancer (CSCC) who cannot have surgery or radiation [14]. At an infusion clinic, the oncologist orders Libtayo (cemiplimab), a human PD-1 antibody given as a 30-minute IV drip every three weeks [14]. Regeneron bought back full global rights to Libtayo from Sanofi in 2022. Its own sales team markets the drug worldwide, books 100% of global sales ($1,452.2 million in FY2025; $550 million in Q3 2026, +51% YoY), and pays Sanofi a single-digit royalty [2, 3]. That same hospital sales team now launches Regeneron's CD20xCD3 bispecific Ordspono in lymphoma and BCMAxCD3 bispecific Lynozyfic in multiple myeloma [15]. Meanwhile, Regeneron's rare-disease and heart drugs add high-margin sales with low extra selling costs [2, 16]. That lineup includes Praluent ($262.5 million U.S. sales in FY2025), Evkeeza, Veopoz, and 2026 FDA approvals Livsayis and Pasatru [2, 16].

web_blocks.mechanism: Defended an aging blockbuster anti-VEGF franchise (Lucentis) against biosimilar and off-label competition by launching a higher-durability, dual-mechanism successor (Vabysmo) with extended 16-week dosing intervals.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: Vabysmo scaled past CHF 3.5B+ in annual sales within three years of launch, offsetting Lucentis biosimilar erosion and preserving Roche's ophthalmology operating margins.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Confirms that in retinal buy-and-bill markets, genuine durability (fewer annual intravitreal injections) drives rapid physician switching—supporting Regeneron's Eylea HD 8 mg defense, provided prefilled syringe supply bottlenecks are resolved.

book_paragraphs: To see how Regeneron actually makes its money, you and I need to strip away the accounting jargon and follow three real patients through the healthcare system. Regeneron reports as one segment, but underneath the hood it runs five distinct commercial engines—and each one touches a different doctor, a different distributor, and a different payer.

Start in a retina clinic in Ohio. A 74-year-old patient walks in with blurry central vision from wet macular degeneration. The doctor confirms fluid behind the retina using an OCT scan and walks to the clinic's own refrigerator to pull a vial of Eylea HD. The clinic bought that vial upfront from McKesson or CuraScript SD, injects it into the eye in ten minutes, and bills Medicare Part B under a permanent J-code at Average Sales Price plus a statutory markup. Why does the doctor choose Eylea HD over cheaper 2 mg biosimilars like Amgen's Pavblu? Because Eylea HD's 8 mg dose lets stable patients stretch intervals out to 16 or 20 weeks—meaning half as many needles in the eye each year. That clinical durability is why Eylea HD surged 62% year-over-year to $699 million in Q3 2026 alone, capturing 64% of Regeneron's $1.1 billion U.S. retinal franchise, while Bayer's ex-U.S. Eylea partnership contributed another $1.42 billion in 2025.

Now walk across town to a pulmonologist's office. A 58-year-old COPD patient keeps landing in the emergency room despite using three inhalers. Blood work confirms type 2 inflammation, and the doctor prescribes Dupixent. No clinic fridge is involved here; a specialty pharmacy like CVS Specialty or Accredo clears insurance prior authorization and ships prefilled pens straight to the patient's doorstep every two weeks. Sanofi books the global sale—$17.81 billion in 2025 and $6.5 billion in Q3 2026 alone—reimburses Regeneron for manufacturing the biologic in Rensselaer and Limerick, and splits the profits. That Sanofi collaboration generated $5.88 billion for Regeneron in 2025, or 41% of total revenue, and jumped 68% year-over-year to $2.72 billion in Q3 2026 once the historical development balance was finally paid off.

book_subsections.title: Oncology, Rare Diseases & The Royalty Tail
paragraphs: Finally, step into a community oncology infusion center. A 68-year-old patient with locally advanced cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma receives a 30-minute IV drip of Libtayo, Regeneron's PD-1 immunotherapy. Unlike Dupixent, where Sanofi leads global commercialization, Regeneron reacquired full global rights to Libtayo in 2022. That means Regeneron's own oncology sales force details the drug worldwide, books 100% of global sales—$1.45 billion in 2025, accelerating to $550 million in Q3 2026, a $2.2 billion annualized run rate—and pays only a single-digit royalty back to Sanofi.

That exact same oncology sales force is now carrying Regeneron's newest hematology bispecifics, Lynozyfic in multiple myeloma and Ordspono in lymphoma, into hospital infusion centers. Add in U.S. Praluent ($262.5 million in 2025) for high cholesterol, ultra-rare therapies Evkeeza and Veopoz, newly approved 2026 medicines Livsayis and Pasatru, and $506 million of high-margin royalties on Ilaris and Arcalyst, and you can see why Regeneron is no longer a one-drug eye company. It is a diversified biopharma portfolio powered by one discovery platform.

book_subsections.title: What the Roche Vabysmo Parallel Teaches Us
paragraphs: When skeptics argue that 2 mg Eylea biosimilars will inevitably crush Regeneron's ophthalmology franchise, look at Roche's playbook with Lucentis and Vabysmo between 2016 and 2024. When Lucentis faced biosimilars, Roche didn't win a price war—it won a durability war by giving retina specialists a 16-week dosing option that kept elderly patients out of the waiting room. Regeneron is running that exact same play with Eylea HD's 20-week label, and Q3 2026's 62% surge proves retina doctors are voting with their syringes.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Why Collaboration Accounting Hides True Scale
book_callouts.text: If you only glance at Regeneron's GAAP revenue line ($14.34 billion in FY2025), you miss the true commercial footprint of its science. Because Sanofi and Bayer book gross sales for Dupixent, Kevzara, and ex-U.S. Eylea, Regeneron's collaboration revenue line is almost pure high-margin profit share plus cost recovery—meaning its economic scale is far larger than its reported top line implies.
